Nicholas Culpeper published this English herbal in 1653 so ordinary people, not just Latin-reading physicians, could learn about native plants. It lists hundreds of plants with where they grow, when to gather them, and how people of his time used them. Culpeper also linked each herb to a planet, a mix of botany and astrology. Read it as history: many of its claims were never tested, and some plants in it are toxic.

Florence Nightingale wrote this short guide in 1859 for anyone caring for the sick at home. Her core advice is fresh air, light, warmth, cleanliness, quiet, good food and close observation of the patient. She argues that many problems blamed on illness actually come from poor care. Much of it still lines up with basic modern caregiving, though nursing science has moved far beyond it.

William Banting, a London undertaker, published this pamphlet in 1863 after losing weight on a diet his surgeon suggested: cutting back bread, sugar, beer and potatoes. It became one of the first popular diet books, and 'banting' turned into slang for dieting. It is an important piece of diet history, not a plan to follow; talk to a doctor before changing how you eat.

Luigi Cornaro, a Venetian nobleman, wrote these essays in the 1500s after poor health in middle age led him to a strict, moderate diet. He credits moderation, regular habits and a calm mind for his long, active old age. The exact amounts he ate are not recommendations. The lasting idea is moderation and steady routine.

Written around 170-180 AD as the Roman emperor's private notes to himself, Meditations is a core text of Stoic philosophy. Its main ideas: focus on what you can control, notice that your judgments shape how events feel, accept change, and treat others with fairness and kindness. These ideas still shape modern thinking about resilience. Philosophy, not medical advice.

In this 1899 talk, psychologist William James argues that many people live with needless tension and hurry. Drawing on his theory that the body's actions shape feelings, he suggests relaxing the muscles, slowing down and acting calm to help feel calm. It is an early, readable look at the mind-body link. Historical psychology, not treatment.

Henry David Thoreau describes living for two years in a small cabin he built near Walden Pond, Massachusetts (1845-1847). He writes about simple living, spending less, paying close attention to nature and living on purpose. It is a classic of American writing on simplicity and nature connection.

John Muir's journal of the summer of 1869, spent with a sheep flock in California's Sierra Nevada, published in 1911. He records plants, animals, weather and his sheer joy at being in the mountains. It helped inspire the American conservation movement and is a model of slowing down to notice nature.

Francis Adams's 1849 English translation of writings credited to Hippocrates, the ancient Greek physician. This volume includes 'On Airs, Waters, and Places', which ties health to climate, water, seasons and surroundings, and treats disease as natural rather than supernatural. Many of its medical ideas, such as the four humors, are long outdated. Read it as the history of medicine.

Samuel Smiles's 1859 bestseller tells short life stories of inventors, artists and workers who succeeded through effort, patience and character. Its message: steady work, self-education and perseverance build a good life. Some views reflect its era, but its focus on habits and persistence still reads well.
